summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) while fuel prices remain high, but actual fuel savings from the work‑from‑home mandate are negligible. Public transport ridership is still about 14% below pre‑pandemic daily levels, and high‑mobility sectors such as logistics and construction pose economic risk and equity concerns.

signals.detail: Although the fuel‑policy component scores 100, only 334,000 L were saved in the first week of the mandate—less than 1% of the modeled 35.7 M L ceiling—indicating that the current WFH policy is not delivering measurable fuel reductions.
Daily PT trips total 1.24 M, roughly 14% below the pre‑COVID daily average of 1.43 M, reflecting a modest lag in ridership recovery despite a ridership component of 72.7 in the MF‑Index.
High mobility scores (85‑95) and HIGH risk ratings in Retail & Services, Logistics, and Construction suggest elevated exposure to congestion, fuel cost volatility, and supply‑chain disruptions.

WFH adoption is uneven: Public & GLCs achieve 60% while Logistics and Construction are below 10%, creating disparity in exposure to fuel price shocks and limiting the policy's fairness across sectors.

RON95 at RM4.27/L (up from RM2.20 in 2019) creates price pressure that could encourage a shift to public transport, yet ridership has not fully rebounded, indicating that additional incentives or service improvements are needed to realize a lasting modal shift.

recommendation: Introduce sector‑targeted WFH incentives for Logistics, Construction and Retail to raise their remote‑work rates to at least 30% within 12 months, coupled with a fuel‑tax rebate for firms that meet the target. Simultaneously, allocate RM200 M to expand PT capacity and fare subsidies to accelerate ridership recovery and capitalize on high fuel prices as a modal‑shift lever.
